def: The loop every change goes round: plan, code, build, test, release, deploy, operate, monitor, and back to plan.
How many changes travel through the process together. Smaller batches ship faster and break less.
A stage-by-stage record of how long a change spent being worked on, and how long it spent waiting.
Four numbers that describe how well a team delivers: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore.
How often a team puts changes into production. A DORA speed metric.
How long a change takes from being committed to running in production. A DORA speed metric.
The share of deployments that cause a problem needing a fix, rollback or hotfix. A DORA stability metric.
How long it takes to recover when a deployment causes a problem. A DORA stability metric.
Service level indicator: something you measure about what users experience, usually good events divided by all events.
Service level objective: the target for an SLI over a window of time, such as 99.9% of orders succeeding over 30 days.
The failure an SLO allows: 100% minus the target. Spent on releases and experiments; when it runs out, the team slows down.
Service level agreement: a promise to customers with a penalty if it's missed. Looser than your internal SLO.
Replacing servers with the new version a few at a time, so the service never stops.
Building a full copy of the environment with the new version, then switching all traffic to it at once. Switching back is instant.
Sending a small share of traffic to a new version first, and growing it only while it behaves as well as the old one.
The rules, written before a canary release starts, for when to stop it and send all traffic back.
Changing a database so old and new versions both work: add the new thing, move the code over, remove the old thing later.
An if in the code whose answer comes from a setting, so a feature can be switched on or off without a deploy.
A flag that turns a misbehaving feature off for everyone at once, with no deploy.
Old feature flags left in the code after their job is done. Each one is a hidden branch nobody tests.
The email address an AWS account was created with. It can do anything, so it's protected with MFA and almost never used.
The AWS service for people's everyday sign-in. It hands out credentials that expire after hours, instead of long-lived keys.
A named bundle of permissions, like AdministratorAccess, that IAM Identity Center gives to people in an account.
An AWS Budgets email sent when your spending passes a threshold. It warns you; it doesn't stop anything.
AWS's free offers. What you get depends on when your account was created. Check Billing and Cost Management, then Free Tier.
A package manager for macOS and Linux, including Ubuntu on Windows through WSL. It installs and updates command-line tools by name.
The aws command: AWS from the terminal. It finds credentials in a fixed order and uses the first it finds.
